title: Enemies
tomorrow: in Jesus' story the poor man has a name. the rich man doesn't. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a welcome that comes before the knowing: angels unawares. Today, the people we know too well, and wish we didn't.
screen: `ANGELS UNAWARES.` → `THE ONES WE KNOW TOO WELL.`

segments.voice: A one-star review with your name in it. A group chat that goes quiet when you walk in. Someone who did real harm and never said sorry. Praying for them can feel impossible, or fake. So is there a way to pray for someone you can't stand yet? Jesus' command has a step in it built for exactly that.
screen: `A ONE-STAR REVIEW, YOUR NAME IN IT.` → `IMPOSSIBLE, OR FAKE?` → `A STEP BUILT FOR THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole verse: “Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” Notice the last step. Warm feelings can take years. Doing good may not be safe, or possible. But prayer is open to someone who can't yet manage a kind word. Jesus gives the reason in the next line: “That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.” And he does it himself; on the cross he prays, “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” Now a neighbor who says it too. The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, reads in Max Müller's translation: “For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule.” The same instinct: hate answered with hate only grows. And one honest difference. Jesus grounds it in God: be like the Father, whose sun rises on everyone, and pray. The Dhammapada calls it an old rule, a law of how hatred works, with no prayer to God in the verse. Two neighbors refusing the same cycle, each for their own reasons. And none of this means pretending harm was fine, or staying near someone who hurts you. If anyone is in danger, getting safe comes first: local emergency help, and someone you trust.
screen: `THE LAST STEP: PRAY.` · `HIS SUN ON THE EVIL AND THE GOOD.` · `A NEIGHBOR: HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `THE FATHER, OR AN OLD RULE.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: On paper, write the first name or just the initial of someone you can't stand yet. Under it, write the one thing you can manage today: pray for them, or simply, I don't wish them harm. Fold the paper, hold it through the sit, and let the feeling be whatever it is.
Enemies. The people who've harmed us or hate us, and the hardest command about them: love, bless, do good, pray.
Hold onto this: pray for them, the one step open even before the feeling comes. Day seventeen-twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 1721 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 40 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES THE POOR MAN GET A NAME?`

howItsDone: Some Christians pray for an enemy by name, even briefly, as Jesus commands in Matthew 5:44; Buddhists recite the Dhammapada's teaching that hatred ceases by love, and some practice loving-kindness toward those who have harmed them.

chat.says: nia sent me a buddhist line: 'hatred ceases by love.' is that the same as 'love your enemies'?
options: Close, not identical. Both answer hate with love; Jesus adds prayer, as children of the Father.
Identical. Every religion teaches the exact same thing, just in different words.
Not related. Buddhism is about staying calm; only Jesus talks about enemies.
chat.meaning: Shared: hatred answered with love (Matthew 5:44; Dhammapada 5). Different: Jesus grounds it in the Father and prayer; the Dhammapada calls it an old rule.
